Patagonia's repair campaign is what inspired me to start repairing my own clothes, they made it look cool. I own two pieces by them (three as of today), and I'm satisfied as hell with the quality. I only recently started seeing some worn-through threads at the cuff (specifically the right one which is my mouse hand) of my five year old organic cotton flannel overshirt that is in otherwise mint condition. I'll slap some reinforcement thread on that cuff and I'm sure this will last me many years to come. The color hasn't faded at all, it's kept it's shape gracefully, I've washed it many times, and this is basically my go-to light jacket for two thirds of the year. And this is arguably "modern" Patagonia, since I bought this (50% off at clearance) only around 2021. I'm always on the hunt for brands that sell lasting quality so I own a bunch of different items from different brands that are supposed to be high quality, but so far this flannel outlasts them all. I even had to start putting a disclaimer on my dating profile that I did in fact own more pieces of clothing than just that flannel, because every good photo of me featured it lmao.
I don't like the microplastics of fleece as much as the next person either though. I've also seen a report by Follow the Money released a few years back that made some devastating claims about the ethicalness of their supply chain and how it wasn't quite as good as they claimed. And very recently they sent a cease-and-desist towards climate activist drag queen Pattie Gonia, who has their branding loosely inspired by Patagonia's, to stop selling any merchandise featuring the sort-of-lookalike logo, which left a really sour taste in my mouth because to me, that shared identity only seemed like it was mutually beneficial for both parties, so it kinda sucked that the big company was going after the more vulnerable, more grassroots, and more marginalized (and increasingly so), party. 
Either way, that didn't stop me from buying a Torrentshell, considering the entire internet claims it's basically the best way to spend your money on a rain jacket, from legacy articles to recent best buy guides. And also every store clerk. And every Reddit comment. No one has much bad to say about it, other than the fact that it's a plastic rain jacket and you simply can't expect that to last into eternity.
My baggies shorts are also nice, really good multi purpose swimwear/hiking/lounging/travelling shorts. Those too have seen quite some wear, and I even tore a little hole in them by sitting on the wrong piece of wood and piercing my ass, including whatever textile was in between my ass and the wood, and that hole has been stable for three years and counting. They have faded in the sunlight, noticably, but then again, not much clothing is really up to the challenge of facing our deadly laser.

I’ve bought a lot of Patagucci. I’ve got some shirts, tees, and pants for climbing which are all organic cotton, and were way before all the cheap high street brands and everyone else started with the “organic" label.
They have pioneered a lot of the technical garments on the market today (e.g. down alternatives like the Micro Puff, polar tech fleece projects like the R1, etc.). I’ve used them for years climbing, and I’m still using them for climbing. Whenever I’ve had a problem I’ve been able to send them for repair free of charge and, although it’s never been necessary for me, I know several folks who have had items replaced after 10 years+ of heavy use. I guess, I now see them like Darn Tough socks: yes, they cost me more per item, but I ultimately buy less because I trust in the quality and guarantee over time of each piece I buy.
I’d love us to cut down on synthetic products and microplastics everywhere but, some products just perform that much better when participating in an activity at a high level.

I disagree with the conclusion on wicking at 8:06. It's likely more of a comfort and style decision rather than moisture management, especially since a lot of my 1990s fleece are hydrophobic.

 I do a lot of winter running and have spent a lot of time on cross country skis. Both activities are a study in moisture management if you are out for over an hour.

 Wicking works well with one layer but less so with many layers. With two or more layers, you just want sweat to evaporate on your skin and move outwards in vapor form, as this will get it as far as possible from your core region and provide responsive cooling (evaporative cooling to regulate temperature is necessary). If two layers are needed, cross country skiers, winter cyclists, and ski mountaineering racers will use a mesh baselayer (either cycling or scandinavian style, depending on the temperature) below the spandex to create loft with minimal skin contact. If spandex isn't used, advanced modern fabrics designed for high exertion activities like Teijin Octa and polar tech alpha direct 60 are high loft, ultra breathable, and have hairlike plastic  fibers facing inwards for minimum skin contact.
